title: A great week for ed reform thanks to Nikole Hannah-Jones
author: Michael J. Petrilli
summary: Michael Petrilli's weekly SCHOOLED issue treats Nikole Hannah-Jones's New York Times Magazine essay about her daughter's failing schools as an opening for the education reform movement. Rather than joining the dunking, he highlights reactions that focused on her reporting, including Coleman Hughes on teachers unions, Eva Moskowitz on sending her own children to Success Academy, and Matt Yglesias on the improvement of D.C. public schools. His central argument is that the obvious lesson of Najya's experience is school reform from inside and outside the system. He then widens the frame to a broader turn toward academic standards, citing outrage over a University of California op-ed, a viral chart linking teachers union strength to weak literacy policy, and Pondiscio and Gibb on England's knowledge-rich curriculum. The issue closes by noting reform plans emerging on the left and a long list of further reactions and edu-opinions.
points: Petrilli argues that the Hannah-Jones essay is uniquely valuable to reformers because she has been a hero to many reform critics.
He singles out responses that dwell on the concrete dysfunction in Najya's schools and show that high-poverty schools need not be terrible.
D.C. Public Schools is offered as evidence that urban districts can improve across all demographic subgroups under sustained reform.
He reads the backlash against lowered standards, from the UC graduation debate to New York's Regents change, as a sign the tide is turning.
The issue notes that curriculum reform is drawing conservative interest and that centrist and progressive groups are drafting their own reform agendas.
quotes: Much of the debate quickly devolved into the typical dunking, defending, and sides-taking. But let that not obscure the opportunity this moment provides for the education reform movement.
Like Waiting for Superman, like “The Rubber Room,” like A Nation at Risk, et al., Hannah-Jones’s piece is an opening to remind the American public that schools matter and can be improved.

To that end, my favorite reactions were those that focused on Nikole’s reporting—the gobsmacking details about the dysfunction in her daughter’s schools. And reminded us that high-poverty schools need not be terrible.

So, yes, we all wish that Nikole had come to the obvious conclusion: The way to fix the schools that failed Najya is to reform the system, from both the inside and the outside. In other words: school reform.

I don’t think it’s hopium to say that the tide is turning when it comes to academic standards. And not just in our little ed-reform bubble. These stories about lowered standards are sparking real outrage, something we haven’t seen in over a decade.
I love it. Also great: They published the article in the National Review, a sign that conservatives are open to curriculum reform, too, not just school choice and culture wars.

We’d better pay attention because many political pundits see a blue wave coming, one that could usher in a Democratic House and Senate, but also more D’s in statehouses than seemed likely just a few months ago.
